chapter-one-brain-map-1/chapter-one-brai.description: Three Specific ContextsPg. 9-12Chapter 1 - Theories of Development & GeneticsTheories of DevelopmentMultidirectional - We don't just grow in one area, and we don't just stay at a standstill either. Humans can grow in multiple areas, in one area, or actually decay or have loss as well.Lifelong - You don't reach 28 years old and stay stuck like that forever. You grow in some ways, lose other things (coughmalepatterbaldnesscoughcough), and that means you can become a totally different individual at 86 or something.Multidimensional: We can change across three different domains or dimensions (not literal); physical, cognitive, and psychosocial.Characterized by Plasticity - How we can accept change basicallyMultidisciplinary - Double Dipping in the party dip but in a Human Development lens. He basically recognizes that people can take multiple perspectives into account.Normative history-graded influences: The period of time in which you were born can have a great deal of importance to your individual characteristics (ex. Baby Boomers -> Talk on Phone, Gen Z -> Life is Phone)Normative age-graded influences: An age grade means stages like toddler or teenagerNon-normative life influences:MulticontextualPsychosocial - How we interact with those around us.Cognitive - Changes in our minds, like learning a new language, or taking a Human Development class :)All three of these Domains interact with each other and change one another. Failure in one can cause others to faulter, and the inverse is also applicable.Physical - Biological development (puberty, major illness).Socioeconomic status is also another context, but Paul Baltes didn't feel like adding it in his list I guess. Socioeconomic just means your place in society and tax brackets (businessman vs ceo) also has an effect on your development.

notes-detailed/behavioral-genetics.html.title: Behavioral Genetics
notes-detailed/behavioral-genetics.html.description:
Behavioral Genetics measure how much of a person's traits are from genes and predisposition, versus how much is from their environment and opportunities (or lack thereof), essentially nature v nurture.
Passive genotype-environment correlation - A child is born into a family that supports athleticism while being naturally athletic. Basically both support a trait.
Evocative genotype-environment correlation - How individual characteristics (being shy, being extroverted, or being unendingly hungry) changes how an environment reacts to them.
Active genotype-environment correlation - natural predisposition to things or natural ability causing people to seek out specific environments to reinforce certain characteristics.
Genotype - Environment Interactions - The inverse of the aforementioned AGEC, where the environment enforces or breaks inherited characteristics.
Epigenetics - The changing of genes themselves due to environmental aspects.

notes-detailed/genes.html.title: Genes
notes-detailed/genes.html.description: Genes are sequences of nucleotides, blueprints for making proteins. Proteins then construct cells and command the functions of them. Genes are located in chromosomes, and there are 20,500 genes in the human body (est.) People gain 23 chromosomes per parent, adding to a total of 46. There are two main aspects of genes are Genotype and Phenotype. When a child inherits too many or too little chromosomes, it's called chromosomal abnormality. This is usually linked to an older mother, as the ovum has been been aged for longer and has a higher chance to mutate. The most common example of chromosomal abnormality is down syndrome.

notes-detailed/genotype.html.title: Genotype
notes-detailed/genotype.html.description: Quite simply the sum total of genes a person inherits. I don't know if they're more complicated than that.

notes-detailed/meiosis.html.title: Meiosis
notes-detailed/meiosis.html.description: The process in which the sexual reproduction cells go through duplication and copy themselves. The first duplication creates a perfect copy, but then they split apart and only have half the genetic material of the original cell.

notes-detailed/mitosis.html.title: Mitosis
notes-detailed/mitosis.html.description: The process in which cells go through duplication and copy themselves. The nucleus of the cell contains the chromosomes of the human, and when going through mitosis they replicate and double perfectly. The the cell splits an creates two identical copies.

notes-detailed/phenotype.html.title: Phenotype
notes-detailed/phenotype.html.description: Phenotypes are the expressed features of a gene. There are dominant genes, where the phenotype they present is presented even when paired with a different version of the gene, and there are recessive genes, where they don't present themselves unless paired with another recessive. These different versions of genes come from having a mix of chromosomes from your mother and father, and when you have the same version of a gene, that called being homozygous, and being different means heterozygous. Different versions of the same genes are called alleles. Most characteristics or phenotypes are polygenic, meaning it's a collaborative effort from multiple genes for the presented phenotype.

info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.
